display_name: Howard Park Leston Shiraz, Margaret River
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The Leston vineyard sits on Margaret River’s ironstone ridge, forcing Shiraz roots to mine through gravel and clay for water that barely reaches 650 mm a year. Howard Park turns that struggle into dark, pepper-spiked plum with the tension of a compressed spring. It’s the bottle that converts Cabernet-drinking locals to Shiraz without them noticing.",
  "wine_summary": "Howard Park was among the first to plant Shiraz on the ridge that bears the Leston name, and they still crop at 6 tonnes/ha, half the regional average, to keep berry size down and skin-to-juice ratio high. The 2016 walks a line that Margaret River rarely allows Shiraz: black-fruit density without the warm-climate jam, thanks to afternoon sea breezes that drop temperatures 8 °C before sunset. The winery’s house style is 18 months in 30 % new French oak, giving cedar lift rather than sweetness, letting the ironstone ferric edge read as cracked pepper and sage.",
  "terroir_expression": "Red gravelly loam shot through with ironstone pebbles drains winter rainfall in days, storing just enough in the clay below to keep vines alive through the bone-dry January–March ripening period. That hydric stress shrinks berries and thickens skins, pumping pyrazines into the juice—the source of the wine’s green peppercorn and eucalyptus top-notes. The ridge’s 180 m elevation lifts the fruit above morning fog, holding acidity while the Indian Ocean’s afternoon breeze prevents sugar accumulation above 14 % alcohol.",
  "vinification_summary": "Fruit is destemmed but not crushed, allowing a portion of whole berries to ferment carbonically, softening Margaret River’s naturally high tannin. Wild-yeast fermentation peaks at 30 °C for eight days, then the wine is pressed to barrel while still 4 g/L residual sugar, completing malolactic fermentation in oak (the technical term is “malolactic in cask”) which rounds acidity and integrates vanilla-lactone oak compounds before the first racking.",
  "food_pairing": "Nashville hot chicken—the wine’s cracked-pepper phenolics mirror the cayenne crust while black fruit cools the burn. Korean charcoal bulgogi wrapped in ssamjang lettuce: soy sweetness picks up the French-oak cedar, while the vine’s sage notes echo sesame oil. Roast porcini-rubbed rib-eye at a steakhouse: ironstone ferric edge marries the mushroom umami, and medium-plus tannin cuts the marbled fat. For vegetarians, charred eggplant involtini with smoked tomato sugo: the wine’s pepper and smoke chase the grill marks, acid keeps tomato bright.",
  "comparable_wines": "Clonakilla Shiraz/Viognier, Canberra — same pepper-spice axis but ups the floral quotient with co-fermented Viognier. Penley Edward’s Reserve Shiraz, Coonawarra — similar iron-earth undertow from terra rossa over limestone, though slightly warmer and plusher. Mount Langi Ghiran Cliff Edge Shiraz, Grampians — shares eucalyptus top-note from cool Victorian nights, but granite soil gives more mineral snap.",
  "style_profile": "Medium-full dry red with firm graphite tannins and ironstone-pepper lift",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 2024–2030; after eight years the pepper cracks and fruit recedes, so stop there. Store at 14 °C, 65 % humidity; screw-cap means no cork failure but lightstrike fades colour—keep it dark.",
  "value_assessment": "A$38–45 locally, US$32–38 import markets. At that bracket it competes with Jim Barry The Lodge Hill and d’Arenberg The Footprint, but Leston gives you estate-grown Margaret River fruit rather than multi-regional blending. Worth the ask: the ridge site is now fully mature so quality is locked in, yet pricing hasn’t tracked the 15 % regional inflation of the last five years.",
  "market_position": "Restaurant by-the-glass staple in Perth bistros because it tastes twice the price; somms pour it for Cabernet regulars who ‘don’t drink Shiraz’. Retail buyers are 30–55 yr professionals who want regional badge without cult-tax; collectors skip it, saving money for Cullen or Leeuwin. Export pallets land in the UK and Canada where Margaret River still carries surf-and-sunshine cachet.",
  "insider_take": "Skip the 2015—wet vintage gave plum jam and lowered the pepper that defines this label; 2016 and 2012 are the sweet spots. Too many drinkers serve it at 20 °C and call it ‘fruity’; drop it to 16 °C and the ironstone tannin wakes up, turning the wine into the black-pepper steak knife it was built to be.",
  "aging_potential_years": 10,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 4,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 10,
  "sensory": {
    "acidity": 4,
    "tannin": 4,
    "body": 4,
    "sweetness": 1,
    "alcohol": 4,
    "color_intensity": "deep",
    "aroma_intensity": "pronounced",
    "finish_length": "long",
    "complexity": "complex",
    "quality_level": "very_good"
  }
}

parsed.hook: The Leston vineyard sits on Margaret River’s ironstone ridge, forcing Shiraz roots to mine through gravel and clay for water that barely reaches 650 mm a year. Howard Park turns that struggle into dark, pepper-spiked plum with the tension of a compressed spring. It’s the bottle that converts Cabernet-drinking locals to Shiraz without them noticing.
parsed.wine_summary: Howard Park was among the first to plant Shiraz on the ridge that bears the Leston name, and they still crop at 6 tonnes/ha, half the regional average, to keep berry size down and skin-to-juice ratio high. The 2016 walks a line that Margaret River rarely allows Shiraz: black-fruit density without the warm-climate jam, thanks to afternoon sea breezes that drop temperatures 8 °C before sunset. The winery’s house style is 18 months in 30 % new French oak, giving cedar lift rather than sweetness, letting the ironstone ferric edge read as cracked pepper and sage.
parsed.terroir_expression: Red gravelly loam shot through with ironstone pebbles drains winter rainfall in days, storing just enough in the clay below to keep vines alive through the bone-dry January–March ripening period. That hydric stress shrinks berries and thickens skins, pumping pyrazines into the juice—the source of the wine’s green peppercorn and eucalyptus top-notes. The ridge’s 180 m elevation lifts the fruit above morning fog, holding acidity while the Indian Ocean’s afternoon breeze prevents sugar accumulation above 14 % alcohol.
parsed.vinification_summary: Fruit is destemmed but not crushed, allowing a portion of whole berries to ferment carbonically, softening Margaret River’s naturally high tannin. Wild-yeast fermentation peaks at 30 °C for eight days, then the wine is pressed to barrel while still 4 g/L residual sugar, completing malolactic fermentation in oak (the technical term is “malolactic in cask”) which rounds acidity and integrates vanilla-lactone oak compounds before the first racking.
parsed.food_pairing: Nashville hot chicken—the wine’s cracked-pepper phenolics mirror the cayenne crust while black fruit cools the burn. Korean charcoal bulgogi wrapped in ssamjang lettuce: soy sweetness picks up the French-oak cedar, while the vine’s sage notes echo sesame oil. Roast porcini-rubbed rib-eye at a steakhouse: ironstone ferric edge marries the mushroom umami, and medium-plus tannin cuts the marbled fat. For vegetarians, charred eggplant involtini with smoked tomato sugo: the wine’s pepper and smoke chase the grill marks, acid keeps tomato bright.
parsed.comparable_wines: Clonakilla Shiraz/Viognier, Canberra — same pepper-spice axis but ups the floral quotient with co-fermented Viognier. Penley Edward’s Reserve Shiraz, Coonawarra — similar iron-earth undertow from terra rossa over limestone, though slightly warmer and plusher. Mount Langi Ghiran Cliff Edge Shiraz, Grampians — shares eucalyptus top-note from cool Victorian nights, but granite soil gives more mineral snap.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-full dry red with firm graphite tannins and ironstone-pepper lift
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2024–2030; after eight years the pepper cracks and fruit recedes, so stop there. Store at 14 °C, 65 % humidity; screw-cap means no cork failure but lightstrike fades colour—keep it dark.
parsed.value_assessment: A$38–45 locally, US$32–38 import markets. At that bracket it competes with Jim Barry The Lodge Hill and d’Arenberg The Footprint, but Leston gives you estate-grown Margaret River fruit rather than multi-regional blending. Worth the ask: the ridge site is now fully mature so quality is locked in, yet pricing hasn’t tracked the 15 % regional inflation of the last five years.
parsed.market_position: Restaurant by-the-glass staple in Perth bistros because it tastes twice the price; somms pour it for Cabernet regulars who ‘don’t drink Shiraz’. Retail buyers are 30–55 yr professionals who want regional badge without cult-tax; collectors skip it, saving money for Cullen or Leeuwin. Export pallets land in the UK and Canada where Margaret River still carries surf-and-sunshine cachet.
parsed.insider_take: Skip the 2015—wet vintage gave plum jam and lowered the pepper that defines this label; 2016 and 2012 are the sweet spots. Too many drinkers serve it at 20 °C and call it ‘fruity’; drop it to 16 °C and the ironstone tannin wakes up, turning the wine into the black-pepper steak knife it was built to be.
